subject: Perimeter origin binding and egress clauses for private endpoints
messages:
From: Raj Singh <raj.singh@kestrel-health.com>
To: Irene Choi <irene_choi@redwood.ai>
Cc: ops@kestrel-health.com, netsec-team@kestrel-health.com
Date: Thu, 5 Apr 2028 15:18:00 -0700
Subject: Private endpoint IP allowlist question / NAT details

Hi Irene,

Thanks again for walking us through the private deployment options earlier. We are finalizing our network design and need a bit of clarity on Redwood's allowlist and egress expectations before we sign off with our network team. Two specific items: 

1) We currently use a NAT pool for outbound traffic where ephemeral ports are translated to a short-lived set of public IPs (rotated nightly via our cloud NAT). Can Redwood accept a small pool of rotating public IPs, or do you require dedicated static addresses per environment?

2) For runtime traffic you reference FQDN-based callbacks in the docs. Our ops team prefers allowing FQDNs (e.g., *.redwood-inference.com) rather than a long list of IPs to reduce operational overhead. Will FQDN allowlisting + TLS/SNI checking be sufficient for private control plane endpoints, or will we still need static egress IPs for audit/compliance?

Also, if there are specific host header or SNI values we should pin, let us know. Attached is our preliminary NAT mapping and current cloud egress design.

Appreciate the guidance — Raj
Kestrel Health — Platform Ops

Attachments: kestrel-nat-design-0404.pdf (attachment stub)

From: Irene Choi <irene_choi@redwood.ai>
To: Raj Singh <raj.singh@kestrel-health.com>
Cc: marissa_cole@redwood.ai, david_kim@redwood.ai
Date: Fri, 6 Apr 2028 09:02:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Private endpoint IP allowlist question / NAT details

Raj — thanks for the clear notes and the NAT sketch. Short answers up front: we prefer static egress for control-plane traffic, but there are mitigations and a hybrid approach that many customers adopt. Details below.

High-level requirements (control plane):
- Control-plane API (account provisioning, health-checking, admin callbacks) must be reachable from a stable set of IPs. We need at least 2 static public IPs for failover.
- TLS required on 443; we validate SNI and Host header. For verification pinning we expect SNI to be the public FQDN you provide to us (e.g., kestrel-control.kestrel-health.com).
- If you cannot provide static IPs, we can run a proxy/egress gateway on your side (or offer a Redwood-managed egress endpoint with dedicated IPs under a Dedicated contract).

Runtime inference traffic (data plane):
- For model inference calls originating in your VPC to private endpoints, FQDN allowlisting + mTLS to the control plane is acceptable as long as:
  * You provide TLS client certs for the control plane (mutual TLS).
  * You agree to preserve X-Request-ID and our outbound fingerprint headers (we will provide exact names).
  * You supply an audit log export showing NAT translations and timestamps for bursts (for SOC2 evidence).

Operational notes and attachments:
- I've attached a short firewall template you can reuse (redwood-firewall-template-v1.docx). It contains the minimal control-plane egress (two IPs/443, outbound DNS to your resolver only, and required NTP).
- For ephemeral pools we require a documented rotation schedule and an automated feed (CSV or API) of current IPs if you rotate more than once per week.

Next steps:
1) If you can provide two static control-plane IPs, list them and we will provision the allowlist on our side.
2) If not, indicate whether you can use mTLS + FQDN for runtime and supply the audit log export cadence — we will escalate to compliance.

I'll loop in David and Marissa internally to confirm audit evidence expectations and any fallback.

— Irene
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

Attachments: redwood-firewall-template-v1.docx (attachment stub)

From: David Kim <david_kim@redwood.ai>
To: Irene Choi <irene_choi@redwood.ai>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>, Jordan Blake <jordan_blake@redwood.ai>
Date: Mon, 9 Apr 2028 10:11:00 -0700
Subject: FW: Private endpoint IP allowlist question / NAT details

Team — quick internal thread so we can advise Kestrel. Two pragmatic options we should propose: 

Option A (preferred for audit simplicity):
- Customer assigns at least two static public IPs for control-plane egress. We'll require IP attestations and a reverse DNS entry (controlplane.kestrel-health.com -> IP).
- Ports: 443 outbound to our control-plane IPs only. DNS outbound only to their resolver (to avoid split-horizon issues).
- Logging: daily NAT translation export and weekly signed attestations for SOC evidence.

Option B (lower operational lift for customer, higher telemetry for us):
- Customer uses FQDN allowlist for data-plane (e.g., *.redwood-inference.com) + mTLS client certs for control-plane auth.
- Customer provides a rotation feed (S3/HTTPS CSV or HubSpot webhook) when IPs change; rotation cadence must be >= 7 days or they accept a temporary exception window.
- Additional: we require per-connection metadata (X-Redwood-Client, X-Request-ID) and flow logs for the NAT gateway retained for 90 days.

Open questions for compliance: what counts as sufficient "audit log export"? Our compliance team will accept Flow logs + signed daily manifest (CSV with mapping) — Marissa, correct?

Irene — if they want hybrid, we can require static IPs for the control plane and FQDN+MTLS for runtime. That minimizes IP burden while keeping control-plane stable.

— David

(quoted original customer email below)

From: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>
To: David Kim <david_kim@redwood.ai>, Irene Choi <irene_choi@redwood.ai>, Jordan Blake <jordan_blake@redwood.ai>, Laura Bennett <laura_bennett@redwood.ai>
Date: Mon, 9 Apr 2028 15:46:00 -0700
Subject: Re: FW: Private endpoint IP allowlist question / NAT details

Agree with David's framing. For customers in regulated health verticals (Kestrel is one) we should aim for a hybrid pattern by default: static control-plane IPs + runtime FQDN + mTLS. That reduces ops friction for the customer while meeting audit. Two operational clarifications before we commit: 

1) Evidence stanza: require daily NAT translation CSV with UTC timestamps, source private CIDR -> NAT IP mapping, and SHA256 signature from their ops account. That will satisfy our SOC2 evidence checklist.
2) FQDN TTLs: recommend customers set DNS TTLs >= 300s for all endpoints used by Redwood; if TTLs are shorter, we mark as high-change and require a rotation feed.

Jordan — please add a short runbook snippet (we'll add to the Confluence page) that steps through emergency IP rotation and temporary allowlist exceptions (15 minute window max with RBAC approver).

Marissa
VP, Product Operations

From: Irene Choi <irene_choi@redwood.ai>
To: Raj Singh <raj.singh@kestrel-health.com>
Cc: ops@kestrel-health.com, netsec-team@kestrel-health.com, marissa_cole@redwood.ai, david_kim@redwood.ai
Date: Tue, 10 Apr 2028 09:34:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Private endpoint IP allowlist question / NAT details — proposal

Raj — following our internal review, here's a concise proposal for Kestrel's private deployment allowlisting and egress controls. We tried to balance auditability and your ops preferences.

Agreed hybrid approach (recommended):
1) Control plane (required static):
   - Provide 2 static public IPs for control-plane egress. Example CSV template attached (perimeter-static-ip-proposal.csv).
   - Redwood will only accept inbound control-plane callbacks from those IPs on 443. SNI must match the FQDN you provide.
   - Provide reverse DNS and a signed daily manifest for initial 30 days; after stabilization weekly attestations are acceptable.

2) Runtime / data plane (FQDN + mTLS):
   - Allowlisting by FQDN for inference endpoints (e.g., runtime-*.redwood-inference.com) is acceptable if you: 
     * Terminate TLS using client certs (we will issue client certs for mTLS).
     * Preserve X-Request-ID and X-Redwood-Client headers.
     * Retain NAT flow logs for 90 days and provide daily CSV export during the onboarding window (first 30 days).

3) Rotation & automation:
   - If you must rotate control-plane IPs more frequently than every 7 days, publish an HTTPS-accessible CSV (or S3) with the new IPs and a SHA256 signature. We will ingest this feed for automated allowlist updates.

4) Ports and services:
   - Outbound ports allowed: 53 (DNS) to your resolver, 123 (NTP), 443 (TLS). All other outbound ports should be explicit and justified.

5) Logging & evidence for audit:
   - NAT translation CSV with UTC timestamps, source private IP, source port, NAT IP, NAT port. Signed by their ops account. 90-day retention minimum.

Next steps:
- Please confirm you can provide two static IPs for control-plane egress or confirm you prefer the managed egress option (we can scope pricing).
- If you accept the hybrid model, attach the completed perimeter-static-ip-proposal.csv and we will schedule a short onboarding call to exchange mTLS certs.

Thanks — we can be flexible on the attestation cadence once we see the initial manifests.

Best,
Irene
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

Attachments: perimeter-static-ip-proposal.csv (attachment stub)
